summary: Automatic drift detection can mistake intentional evolution or vague aspirations for defects, and maintaining trace links may cost more than updating the underlying documents.

points.text: Natural-language specifications are incomplete and often deliberately aspirational; semantic similarity cannot reliably determine whether a code difference is a violation or an accepted implementation choice.
Specifications, tests and code can all be wrong, so declaring one artifact the comparison authority may synchronize the system to an obsolete requirement.
Requirement-to-code links are costly to create and update across refactors, and stale links can produce more noise than having no automatic comparison.
Teams may optimize a drift score by deleting detailed commitments or adding vague documentation rather than resolving the underlying architectural disagreement.
